documents.content:
# Load Store Unit (LSUv3) ![LSUv3 Architecture](../images/lsu.svg) The Load Store Unit (LSU) executes memory operations for scalar, floating-point, vector (RVV), and matrix/tile (VME) instructions. It translates decoded operations into memory transactions across tightly-coupled memories (TCM) and external system busses while managing coalescing, ordering, fault reporting, and register writeback. ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph Decode & Dispatch REQ["io.req[0..L-1] (LsuCmd)"] --> ALIGN["Aligner"] ALIGN --> RS["Reservation Station (rs)
CircularBufferMulti"] end subgraph Execution: LsuSuperSlot RS -->|io.uop| SS["LsuSuperSlot (State Machine)"] CELLS["LsuCell Array
nCells: 8 × VLENB (or 4 bytes)"] <--> SS RVV_IN["rvv2lsu / vme2lsu
(Indices, Store Data, Masks)"] --> SS SS --> WIN["Sliding Window Bundler
(Normal vs. Strict Mode)"] end subgraph Bus Interface & Coalescing WIN --> ARB["Bus Arbiter & Address Decoder"] ARB -->|Reads Only| IBUS["IBus (ITCM)"] ARB -->|16B Rows| DBUS["DBus (DTCM)"] ARB -->|Variable Size| EBUS["EBus (External / Peripheral)"] end subgraph Response & Writeback IBUS & DBUS & EBUS -->|Bus Responses & Snooping| SS SS -->|Scalar Int| RD["io.rd (Scalar Regfile)"] SS -->|Scalar Float| RDFLT["io.rd_flt (Float Regfile)"] SS -->|Vector Streaming| RVV_OUT["io.lsu2rvv / io.lsu2vme"] SS -->|Drained / Completed| STORE_DONE["io.storeComplete"] end ``` ## Pipeline Overview The LSU operates as a decoupled, in-order execution pipeline: 1. **Ingestion & Pointer-Chasing (`LsuUOp`)**: Decodes up to `p.instructionLanes` commands (`LsuCmd`) per cycle, fetching base addresses and store data from the scalar/floating-point register file bus ports (`io.busPort`, `io.busPort_flt`). 2. **Reservation Station (`rs`)**: Dispatched micro-operations are packed by an `Aligner` and stored in a multi-lane circular buffer (`CircularBufferMulti`) to buffer commands ahead of execution. 3. **Execution Engine (`LsuSuperSlot`)**: Dequeues a single `LsuUOp` at a time and instantiates an array of byte-level tracking cells (`LsuCell`) sized to the maximum architectural vector register group ($8 \times \text{VLENB}$, or 4 bytes for scalar configurations). 4. **Windowed Bus Bundling**: Scans active cells using a sliding window (`windowSizeNormal` or `windowSizeStrict`), bundling matching row addresses into coalesced 16-byte (`p.lsuDataBytes`) memory transactions. 5. **Writeback & Streaming**: Routes read responses back into cells (with single-cycle response snooping across identical rows) and streams completed elements to scalar writeback ports or the vector core (`io.lsu2rvv`). ## Ingestion & Reservation Station (`rs`) ### Multi-Lane Ingestion & Alignment The core dispatch unit presents up to `p.instructionLanes` decoupled memory commands (`io.req`) per cycle. - **Capacity Check**: A prefix-sum scan (`validSums`) checks against `rs.io.nSpace` to determine how many commands can be accepted. Remaining lanes are backpressured (`req(i).ready = false`). - **Operand Fetch**: Base register address generation and store data bypassing occur in parallel using `RegfileBusPortIO`. - **`LsuUOp` Generation**: Computes initial byte-level memory bounds (prestart `startCell = vstart × NF × EEW`, active elements `[startCell, endCell)` with `endCell = vl × NF × EEW`, and unreachable tail bounds `[endCell, unreachableCell)` with `unreachableCell = LMUL × NF × VLENB`), stride multipliers (`bytesPerSegment`), and vector addressing modes from `io.rvvState` (`vtype`, `vl`, `vstart`). - **Alignment**: The `Aligner` packs sparse valid dispatches into dense circular buffer inputs. ### Circular Buffer (`CircularBufferMulti`) The reservation station buffers up to `max(4, p.instructionLanes)` micro-operations. - It exposes current queue occupancy via `io.queueCapacity`. - Flushed synchronously when `io.pipelineFlush` asserts or on an unrecoverable memory fault. ## `LsuSuperSlot` & `LsuCell` Array `LsuSuperSlot` coordinates all memory bus transactions, RVV handshakes, and register writebacks for the actively executing instruction. ### The `LsuCell` Array Execution is partitioned across `nCells` byte cells ($8 \times \text{VLENB}$ with RVV enabled, or 4 for scalar-only): ```text Cell Index: [ 0 ... startCell ) | [ startCell ... endCell ) | [ endCell ... unreach ) | [ unreach ... nCells ) |< Prestart (Inactive) >|< Active Elements >|< Tail (Inactive) >|< Unallocated (DONE) >| [0, startCell) [startCell, endCell) [endCell, unreach) [unreach, nCells) ``` Each `LsuCell` stores: - `state`: Current lifecycle state (`LsuCellState`). - `data`: 8-bit data payload. - `rowAddr`: Memory row address (`addr >> dbusOffsetBits`). - `mask`: One-hot byte position within the 16-byte bus row. ### Cell Lifecycle (`LsuCellState`) - **`DONE`**: Cell is idle, unallocated (`[unreachableCell, nCells)`), or has finished writeback. - **`W_DATA`**: Waiting for vector element index (`rvv2lsu.idx`), store data (`rvv2lsu.vregfile`), or mask bit (`rvv2lsu.mask`). Masked-off elements (`mask == 0`) transition directly to `W_WB`. - **`W_START`**: Address and store data are valid; ready to participate in a bus transaction. - **`W_RESP`**: Bus request issued; awaiting bus response data. - **`W_WB`**: Data returned from memory (or skipped); awaiting scalar writeback or vector writeback stream acknowledgment. Inactive elements (both prestart elements `[0, startCell)` and tail elements `[endCell, unreachableCell)`) initialize directly to `W_WB` (or `DONE` for tile stores), skipping memory transactions. ### Address Generation Paths 1. **Continuous (Scalar & Unit-Stride Vector)**: Base row address and byte offsets are pre-computed using a consecutive row lookup table (`rowTable`), allowing immediate parallel initialization of all cell row addresses. 2. **Strided (RVV)**: Uses a 16-entry lookup table (`makeStridedOffsets`) for supported element/segment multipliers ($1, 2, \dots, 32$) scaled by stride ($rs2$). 3. **Indexed (RVV)**: Base address is updated dynamically per element as index vectors arrive over `rvv2lsu.idx`. ## Bus Transaction Bundling & Memory Modes CoralNPU bus transactions are aligned to 16-byte rows (`p.lsuDataBytes`). `LsuSuperSlot` maintains a sliding window of cells starting at `leadIndex`: ### Normal Mode (Coalesced & Snooped) - Examines up to `windowSizeNormal` (16) cells ahead of `leadIndex`. - Coalesces all cells targeting the same `rowAddr` into a single bus transaction with an aggregated byte mask (`wmask`) and write data (`wdata`). - Services all standard memory operations not requiring strict element serialization: - Scalar integer and floating-point loads/stores. - Unit-stride vector loads/stores (including masked and whole-register variants). - Unordered indexed vector operations (`VLOAD_UINDEXED`, `VSTORE_UINDEXED`). - Non-zero strided vector operations (`VLOAD_STRIDED`, `VSTORE_STRIDED`). - Unconstrained zero-stride vector operations where `rs2 == x0`. Per the RISC-V Vector specification, strided instructions encoding `rs2 == x0` permit combining multiple elements into fewer memory accesses. - Matrix/tile operations (`VTLOAD`, `VTSTORE` under VME). - **Response Snooping**: On read responses, all cells in the slot matching `respRowAddr` in states `W_START` or `W_RESP` capture data in parallel, drastically reducing bus bandwidth for duplicate or clustered accesses. ### Strict Mode (Spec-Ordered Execution) - Engaged exclusively for operations requiring strict element-ordered execution: - Ordered indexed vector operations (`VLOAD_OINDEXED`, `VSTORE_OINDEXED`). - Constrained zero-stride vector operations where a non-zero register holds zero (`rs2 != x0` and `Reg[rs2] == 0`). While `rs2 == x0` permits coalescing in Normal Mode, the RVV specification mandates that non-`x0` registers with value zero must preserve element order without combining accesses. - Enforces strict serial memory ordering within the active window (`windowSizeStrict`) as required by the RISC-V Vector specification, ensuring earlier vector elements perform their bus transactions before later elements in the same row rather than being coalesced. ### Scalar Cross-Row Accesses Scalar memory accesses execute through Normal Mode. If a scalar load or store crosses a 16-byte row boundary, it is split into at most two naturally aligned power-of-two bus transfers (`tx1Size` and `tx2Size`) precomputed during instruction initialization (`computeScalarTxPlan`): - `tx1`: Naturally aligned transfer for residual bytes in row 1 ending at the row boundary (or the entire access if within a single row). - `tx2`: Naturally aligned transfer for remaining bytes in row 2 starting at offset 0. ## Subsystem Busses The LSU routes memory transactions to three distinct destinations based on physical address mapping: | Subsystem | Port | Access Type | Description | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Instruction TCM** | `io.ibus` | Read-only | Instruction TCM accesses. Writes to ITCM are trapped as faults (`ibusFault`). | | **Data TCM** | `io.dbus` | Read / Write | Point-to-point 16-byte fixed-size interface to DTCM. Zero wait-state pipelined responses. | | **External Memory** | `io.ebus` | Read / Write | External memory / peripheral transactions (AXI/TileLink). Supports sub-row transaction sizes and external bus fault reporting (`ebus.fault`). | ## Pipeline Synchronization & Fault Handling ### `FENCE` & Total Store Order CoralNPU guarantees total memory order across all execution lanes in hardware. Standard `FENCE` instructions are recognized as NOPs at dispatch and retire immediately without stalling the pipeline. ### `FENCE.I` (Instruction Cache / Fetch Sync) - Recognized on lane 0 (`LsuOp.FENCEI`). - Allocates `FlushCmd` with `pcNext = pc + 4`. - Awaits complete drainage of all in-flight store transactions in `LsuSuperSlot`. - Directly pulses `io.flush` (`IFlushIO`) to instruction fetch (`fetch.io.iflush`), redirecting fetch to `pcNext`. ### Fault Reporting Memory faults (DTCM access violation, ITCM write violation, or external bus slave errors) trigger precise architectural traps: - Further transaction dispatch is frozen. - `rs` is flushed (`rs.io.flush`). - For vector operations, `faultingVstart` calculates the exact failing element index: $$\text{vstart} = \frac{\text{faultingCell}}{\text{NF} + 1} \gg \log_2(\text{elementBytes})$$ - Latches precise fault info on `io.fault` (`valid`, `epc`, `addr`, `write`, `vstart`). ## Interface Reference ### Core & Dispatch Interfaces | Signal | Direction | Type | Description | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | `io.req[L]` | Input | `Vec(L, Decoupled(LsuCmd))` | Incoming instruction commands across $L$ dispatch lanes. | | `io.busPort` | Input | `RegfileBusPortIO` | Integer register file read port for base addresses and store data. | | `io.busPort_flt` | Input | `RegfileBusPortIO` | Floating-point register file read port for store data (optional). | | `io.queueCapacity`| Output | `UInt(3.W)` | Available capacity in the circular reservation station. | | `io.pipelineFlush`| Input | `Bool` | Global pipeline flush signal from branch/trap unit. | | `io.active` | Output | `Bool` | High if LSU has queued or executing instructions. | | `io.storeComplete`| Output | `Valid(UInt(32.W))` | Pulses with PC when a store instruction fully commits. | ### Memory Bus Interfaces | Port | Signals | Description | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | `io.ibus` | `valid`, `ready`, `addr`, `rdata` | Read-only access to ITCM memory. | | `io.dbus` | `valid`, `ready`, `write`, `addr`, `adrx`, `size`, `pc`, `wdata`, `wmask`, `rdata` | Point-to-point interface to DTCM (16-byte transfers). | | `io.ebus` | `dbus` (same as above), `fault`, `internal` | Interface to external bus bridge / peripherals with fault detection. | | `io.flush` | `valid`, `ready`, `pcNext` | Flush handshake (`IFlushIO`) wired to `fetch.io.iflush`. | | `io.fault` | `valid`, `bits` (`LsuFaultInfo`) | Precise trap info: faulting PC, address, write flag, and vector `vstart`. | ### Writeback & Extension Interfaces | Port | Direction | Type | Description | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | `io.rd` | Output | `Valid(RegfileWriteDataIO)` | Integer scalar register file writeback. | | `io.rd_flt` | Output | `Valid(FloatRegfileWriteDataIO)` | Floating-point scalar register file writeback. | | `io.rvv2lsu[2]` | Input | `Vec(2, Decoupled(Rvv2Lsu))` | Vector core streams: vector store data, index vectors, and masks. | | `io.lsu2rvv[2]` | Output | `Vec(2, Decoupled(Lsu2Rvv))` | Vector writeback data stream and store completion acknowledgments. | | `io.rvvState` | Input | `Valid(RvvConfigState)` | Dynamic RVV architectural state (`sew`, `lmul`, `vl`, `vstart`). | | `io.vme2lsu` / `io.lsu2vme` | I/O | `Decoupled` | Streaming interface for matrix/tile operations (VME). |

documents.content:
# Debug Module

## Overview

The debug module implements a subset of the RISC-V Debug Specification, providing external debug support for the CoralNPU core. It allows a debugger to halt, resume, and single-step the core, as well as read and write core registers and memory.

## Architecture

The debug module is a standalone module that connects to the core via a dedicated debug interface. It communicates with an external debugger through a simple request/response protocol.

The following diagram illustrates the high-level architecture of the debug module:

![Debug Module Architecture](debug_arch.png)

## Interfaces

The following table describes the internal hardware interfaces of the debug module:

| Name           | Direction | Type                  | Width | Description                               |
|----------------|-----------|-----------------------|-------|-------------------------------------------|
| **ext.req**    | Input     | Decoupled             |       | External debugger request.                |
| ↳ `valid`      |           | Bool                  | 1     | The request is valid.                     |
| ↳ `ready`      |           | Bool                  | 1     | The module is ready for a request.        |
| ↳ `bits`       |           | DebugModuleReqIO      |       | The request payload.                      |
|   ↳ `address`  |           | UInt                  | 32    | The address of the register to access.    |
|   ↳ `data`     |           | UInt                  | 32    | The data to write.                        |
|   ↳ `op`       |           | DmReqOp               | 2     | The operation to perform (NOP, READ, WRITE).|
| **ext.rsp**    | Output    | Decoupled             |       | External debugger response.               |
| ↳ `valid`      |           | Bool                  | 1     | The response is valid.                    |
| ↳ `ready`      |           | Bool                  | 1     | The debugger is ready for a response.     |
| ↳ `bits`       |           | DebugModuleRspIO      |       | The response payload.                     |
|   ↳ `data`     |           | UInt                  | 32    | The data read from the register.          |
|   ↳ `op`       |           | DmRspOp               | 2     | The result of the operation (SUCCESS, FAILED, BUSY).|
| **csr**        | Output    | Valid                 |       | CSR command.                              |
| ↳ `valid`      |           | Bool                  | 1     | The command is valid.                     |
| ↳ `bits`       |           | CsrCmd                |       | The command payload.                      |
| **csr_rd**     | Input     | Valid                 |       | CSR read data.                            |
| ↳ `valid`      |           | Bool                  | 1     | The read data is valid.                   |
| ↳ `bits`       |           | UInt                  | 32    | The read data.                            |
| **scalar_rd**  | Output    | Decoupled             |       | Scalar register file write command.       |
| ↳ `valid`      |           | Bool                  | 1     | The write command is valid.               |
| ↳ `ready`      |           | Bool                  | 1     | The register file is ready.               |
| ↳ `bits`       |           | RegfileWriteDataIO    |       | The write command payload.                |
| **scalar_rs**  |           | Bundle                |       | Scalar register file read interface.      |
| ↳ `idx`        | Output    | UInt                  | 5     | Scalar register file read address.        |
| ↳ `data`       | Input     | UInt                  | 32    | Scalar register file read data.           |
| **float_rd**   | Output    | Valid                 |       | Floating-point register file write command.|
| ↳ `valid`      |           | Bool                  | 1     | The write command is valid.               |
| ↳ `bits`       |           | FRegfileWrite         |       | The write command payload.                |
| **float_rs**   |           | Bundle                |       | Floating-point register file read interface.|
| ↳ `valid`      | Input     | Bool                  | 1     | Floating-point register file read valid.  |
| ↳ `addr`       | Input     | UInt                  | 5     | Floating-point register file read address.|
| ↳ `data`       | Input     | UInt                  | 32    | Floating-point register file read data.   |
| haltreq        | Output    | Bool                  | 1     | Request to halt the core.                 |
| resumereq      | Output    | Bool                  | 1     | Request to resume the core.               |
| resumeack      | Input     | Bool                  | 1     | Core has resumed.                         |
| ndmreset       | Output    | Bool                  | 1     | Reset the debug module.                   |
| halted         | Input     | Bool                  | 1     | Core is halted.                           |
| running        | Input     | Bool                  | 1     | Core is running.                          |
| havereset      | Input     | Bool                  | 1     | Core has been reset.                      |

## Command Protocol

An external debugger communicates with the debug module by reading and writing a set of memory-mapped Control and Status Registers (CSRs) over the AXI interface. These CSRs provide a communication channel to the debug module's internal registers.

### Write Operation

To write to an internal debug module register (e.g., writing `0x1` to `dmcontrol` at address `0x10`):

1. **Poll for readiness:** Read the `status` CSR at `0x31014` and wait for bit 0 to be `1`.
2. **Set address:** Write the target internal register address (`0x10`) to the `req_addr` CSR at `0x31000`.
3. **Set data:** Write the data (`0x1`) to the `req_data` CSR at `0x31004`.
4. **Initiate write:** Write the `WRITE` operation code (`2`) to the `req_op` CSR at `0x31008`.
5. **Poll for response:** Read the `status` CSR at `0x31014` and wait for bit 1 to be `1`.
6. **Check status:** Read the `rsp_op` CSR at `0x31010` to confirm the operation was successful.
7. **Acknowledge response:** Write to the `status` CSR at `0x31014` to clear the response.

### Read Operation

To read from an internal debug module register (e.g., reading from `dmstatus` at address `0x11`):

1. **Poll for readiness:** Read the `status` CSR at `0x31014` and wait for bit 0 to be `1`.
2. **Set address:** Write the target internal register address (`0x11`) to the `req_addr` CSR at `0x31000`.
3. **Initiate read:** Write the `READ` operation code (`1`) to the `req_op` CSR at `0x31008`.
4. **Poll for response:** Read the `status` CSR at `0x31014` and wait for bit 1 to be `1`.
5. **Check status:** Read the `rsp_op` CSR at `0x31010` to confirm the operation was successful.
6. **Read data:** Read the result from the `rsp_data` CSR at `0x3100c`.
7. **Acknowledge response:** Write to the `status` CSR at `0x31014` to clear the response.

## AXI CSR Interface

These registers are mapped into the CoralNPU CSR address space and are used to communicate with the debug module.

| Address    | Name       | Description                                                                                                |
|------------|------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 0x30800    | req_addr   | Write the target debug module register address here.                                                       |
| 0x30804    | req_data   | Write data for the debug module operation here.                                                            |
| 0x30808    | req_op     | Write the operation type (e.g., READ, WRITE) to this register to initiate a debug module command.          |
| 0x3080c    | rsp_data   | After a command completes, the data result is available here.                                              |
| 0x30810    | rsp_op     | After a command completes, the status result (e.g., SUCCESS, FAILED) is available here.                    |
| 0x30814    | status     | A read-only register to check the status of the debug module. Bit 0 indicates if the module is ready for a new request. Bit 1 indicates if a response is available. |

## Internal Debug Module Registers

The debug module implements a set of internal registers that are accessible to an external debugger via the AXI CSR interface. These registers are used to control and monitor the core.

| Address | Name         | Description                               |
|---------|--------------|-------------------------------------------|
| 0x04    | data0        | Data register for abstract commands.      |
| 0x10    | dmcontrol    | Debug module control register.            |
| 0x11    | dmstatus     | Debug module status register.             |
| 0x12    | hartinfo     | Hart information register.                |
| 0x16    | abstractcs   | Abstract command status register.         |
| 0x17    | command      | Abstract command register.                |

### dmcontrol (0x10)

The `dmcontrol` register is used to control the debug module and the core.

| Bits  | Name      | Description                                                                 |
|-------|-----------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 31    | haltreq   | Request to halt the core.                                                   |
| 30    | resumereq | Request to resume the core.                                                 |
| 29:2  | reserved  | Reserved for future use.                                                    |
| 1     | ndmreset  | Reset the debug module.                                                     |
| 0     | dmactive  | Activate the debug module.                                                  |

### dmstatus (0x11)

The `dmstatus` register provides the status of the debug module and the core.

| Bits  | Name       | Description                                                                 |
|-------|------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 11    | allrunning | All harts are running.                                                      |
| 10    | anyrunning | Any hart is running.                                                        |
| 9     | allhalted  | All harts are halted.                                                       |
| 8     | anyhalted  | Any hart is halted.                                                         |
| 7:4   | reserved   | Reserved for future use.                                                    |
| 3:0   | version    | Debug module version.                                                       |

### abstractcs (0x16)

The `abstractcs` register provides the status of abstract commands.

| Bits  | Name     | Description                                                                 |
|-------|----------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 12    | busy     | The abstract command is currently executing.                                |
| 11    | reserved | Reserved for future use.                                                    |
| 10:8  | cmderr   | Abstract command error code.                                                |
| 7:0   | reserved | Reserved for future use.                                                    |

### command (0x17)

The `command` register is used to issue abstract commands to the core.

| Bits    | Name      | Description                                                                 |
|---------|-----------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 31:24   | cmdtype   | The type of abstract command.                                               |
| 23:0    | control   | Command-specific control information.                                       |

## Abstract Commands

Abstract commands are used to perform complex operations on the core, such as reading and writing registers.

To issue an abstract command, the debugger writes to the `command` register. The `cmdtype` field specifies the type of command, and the `control` field contains command-specific information.

### Access Register Command (cmdtype=0)

The Access Register command is used to read and write core registers.

The `control` field for the Access Register command is formatted as follows:

| Bits    | Name      | Description                                                                 |
|---------|-----------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 16      | write     | 1 for a write, 0 for a read.                                                |
| 15:0    | regno     | The number of the register to access.                                       |

The register numbers are defined as follows:

* `0x0000-0x0FFF`: CSRs
* `0x1000-0x101F`: Scalar GPRs
* `0x1020-0x103F`: Floating-point GPRs

## Command Examples

### Reading a GPR (a0)

1. **Issue the read command:** Write to the `command` register (address `0x17`) with the following value:
  * `cmdtype` (bits 31:24): `0x0` (Access Register)
  * `write` (bit 16): `0` (read)
  * `regno` (bits 15:0): `0x100A` (for `a0`)
2. **Wait for completion:** Poll the `abstractcs` register (address `0x16`) until the `busy` bit (bit 12) is cleared.
3. **Check for errors:** Read the `abstractcs` register again and check that the `cmderr` field (bits 10:8) is `0`.
4. **Read the result:** If there are no errors, read the value of GPR `a0` from the `data0` register (address `0x04`).

### Writing a GPR (a0)

1. **Write the value:** Write the desired value for GPR `a0` to the `data0` register (address `0x04`).
2. **Issue the write command:** Write to the `command` register (address `0x17`) with the following value:
  * `cmdtype` (bits 31:24): `0x0` (Access Register)
  * `write` (bit 16): `1` (write)
  * `regno` (bits 15:0): `0x100A` (for `a0`)
3. **Wait for completion:** Poll the `abstractcs` register (address `0x16`) until the `busy` bit (bit 12) is cleared.
4. **Check for errors:** Read the `abstractcs` register again and check that the `cmderr` field (bits 10:8) is `0`.

documents.content:
# Memory ordering, FENCE.TSO and retirement in Cadence

This authored exercise is inspired by public CoralNPU issue #130. Implement
the independent standard-SystemVerilog subsystem `coral_memory_order_subsystem` defined completely by
`cadence_contract.md` and its interface-only assets under `contracts/`. The focus
is exact FENCE.TSO legality, required memory order edges, tagged responses, precise retirement and flush/drain behavior. It is not an upstream whole-core repair or a bit-exact CoralNPU port.

Read the shared module graph, the complete Cadence contract and the source scope
policy before deriving the RTL microarchitecture or TP/UVM. The two tracks must
use the same interface and configuration revision. Original upstream documents
remain unchanged and attributed; they are broader context, not permission to
expand the selected instruction/operation subset. The full original repository,
Scala/Chisel/firtool, Bazel, FuseSoC, Cocotb, Verilator, MPACT, ELF programs and a
RISC-V compiler are not required for any stage of this exercise.

`baseline/` preserves historical source bytes behind the reported issue. Those
files are not a compilable candidate seed and must not be added to the candidate
file list. Build a new SV implementation of the declared boundary. Do not use
the separately held upstream patch or reference implementation as the behavioral
oracle for the new subsystem. Its oracle is the authored contract and applicable
ISA clauses, implemented independently in the UVM scoreboard and assertions.

Required outputs are shared requirements/contracts, a microarchitecture and
synthesizable SV RTL, a source-derived TP, pure-SV UVM agents/sequences/monitors,
independent scoreboards, SVA, covergroups, constraints and complete ordered
filelists. The supplied packages and port includes define interfaces only;
they are not a DUT, a stimulus generator or a reference model.

On the Cadence host use Xcelium for SV/UVM simulation, IMC for native coverage,
Jasper Superlint/CDC/FPV for the corresponding static/formal obligations and
Genus for synthesizability. The staged `eda/cadence_runner.py` offers
inspect/plan/run, `eda/project.example.json` shows the candidate inventory and
`eda/verification_profile.json` is the profile_path for `dv_generate_uvm`.
Materialize the actual candidate configuration as `eda/project.json`. Tool
versions/licenses and command compatibility are checked on the EDA host.

Freeze the applicable functional-bin denominator before regression and require
more than 90%, all mandatory directed obligations and negative/mutation checks,
with no unexpected UVM/SVA failures. Code, toggle and assertion metrics remain
separate. A tool exit or LoopX event completion is not functional acceptance.
Record raw reports/databases, seeds, tool versions and source/constraint/model
hashes. No Cadence compilation, simulation, CDC/formal proof or measured coverage
is claimed by this packaged question.

Independent original source bodies exceed 512 KiB without duplicate documents
or authored padding. That is a context-size measure, NOT implemented requirement
bytes. The case intentionally retains broader ISA/history for scope reasoning.

documents.title: case-scope-policy
documents.content:
# Scope policy: independent Cadence subsystem

The acceptance target is `coral_memory_order_subsystem`, the authored standalone SV boundary in
case-cadence-contract (`cadence_contract.md`), not the original Coral whole core.
The Cadence contract defines exact ports, widths, clocks/resets, supported
operations, memory handshakes, fault/flush rules and liveness assumptions.
It accompanies original source fragments as mandatory source adjudication.
Derive obligations from that contract plus applicable ISA clauses; source size
is broader context, NOT implemented requirement bytes.

Coral issue #130, its original source and pinned correction explain the
historical symptom. They are not a required RTL dependency or a golden model.
Do not require the original repository, Chisel/firtool, Bazel, Cocotb, Verilator,
MPACT, a RISC-V compiler or ELF execution. Candidate RTL/TB is standard SV/UVM
with an explicit closure and executes on Cadence Xcelium/IMC, Jasper and Genus.
The baseline/ files are historical_mechanism_reference only; they are excluded
from the candidate compile inventory. Missing native build tools do not block
this new exercise; missing candidate RTL, valid constraints or Cadence licenses
are reported honestly and never counted as successful execution.

Zero-element compliance is background, NOT an additional repair target.
There is no vector opcode in this standalone decoder. The selected scalar and
fence encodings are exactly M03. FENCE.TSO requires R->R, R->W and W->W order;
stronger full RW,RW serialization is legal. Do not require optional W->R
reordering to occur or count its absence as a missing mandatory coverage bin.

Never turn descriptive examples, unsupported extensions, full-chip software or
upstream build recipes into new implementation obligations. Preserve concrete
ambiguities locally. Coverage requires frozen applicable bins and actual native
Cadence evidence; these authored scope decisions are not simulation evidence.

documents.content:
# Cadence contract: memory ordering, fence decode and retirement

This authored independent SystemVerilog exercise is inspired by CoralNPU issue
#130; it is not a port or a bit-exact reproduction of the original core. Build
`coral_memory_order_subsystem` from this contract and the applicable ISA clauses.
The original Scala/Chisel decoder and upstream patch are historical mechanism
references only. Scala, Chisel/firtool, Bazel, MPACT, Cocotb, Verilator, the full
Coral repository, ELF generation and a RISC-V compiler are not build or
acceptance dependencies. A pure-SV UVM producer supplies instruction words and
operand values directly; no instruction fetch unit or full CPU is required.

## M01. Shared design and verification decomposition

Use instruction/configuration snapshot, legal decode, load/store address and
alignment checking, memory-order tracking, tagged response tracking, completion
buffering and ordered retirement. `module_graph.json` is shared by RTL and
TP/UVM. Physical modules may be merged, but every listed obligation remains.
The producer and byte-addressed memory BFM are external environment boundaries.
Decode exact supported encodings; do not fix the known symptom by globally
disabling illegal-instruction traps or accepting every MISC-MEM instruction.

## M02. Static interface and handshake contract

Compile `contracts/coral_memory_order_contract_pkg.sv` before the DUT; the top
uses `contracts/coral_memory_order_ports.svh`. These assets contain only types
and a port list, not an implementation or a scoreboard. The fixed profile has
XLEN=32, four accepted command slots, four outstanding read transactions,
8-bit command tags and 8-bit memory IDs. One rising-edge clock `clk_i` runs at
10 ns in simulation; this timing choice is not a silicon performance claim.
Active-low `rst_ni` asserts asynchronously and releases synchronously after two
edges. Reset clears all valid outputs and internal tracking; the environment
discards outstanding responses from the old reset epoch.

Ports are `clk_i`, `rst_ni`, `flush_i`, command input `cmd_valid_i`, `cmd_ready_o`,
`cmd_i`; memory output `mem_req_valid_o`, `mem_req_ready_i`, `mem_req_o`; memory
response input `mem_rsp_valid_i`, `mem_rsp_ready_o`, `mem_rsp_i`; and retirement
output `retire_valid_o`, `retire_ready_i`, `retire_o`. Types and widths are
normative in the package. Except reset/flush cancellation, valid and payload
remain stable while stalled. All transfers occur at valid/ready rising edges.
The DUT holds `mem_rsp_ready_o=1` outside reset by reserving a response slot
for each issued ID. The BFM may delay or reorder responses, never duplicate an
ID, and returns data/error only for an issued request. Command tags are unique
until retirement and associated drains complete; memory IDs are unique until
their response. Reuse after completion is legal and must be tested.

Each accepted command snapshots `tag`, `pc`, raw 32-bit `instruction`, `rs1`
and `rs2` values. The producer supplies correctly forwarded operand values for
its program stream; fetch, physical register-file hazards and instruction-cache
coherence are outside this subsystem. The DUT performs decode, effective-address
generation, memory operation, fence ordering and the defined retirement effects.
No result is inferred from a successful simulator exit.

## M03. Instruction and exception subset

Support RV32I ADDI, ADD, LB/LH/LW/LBU/LHU, SB/SH/SW, ordinary FENCE and the exact
FENCE.TSO encoding `32'h8330000f`. ADD/ADDI arithmetic wraps at 32 bits. Decode
opcode/funct3/funct7 correctly. Load effective address is rs1+sign-extended I
immediate; store address is rs1+sign-extended S immediate. The destination is
instruction rd; rd=x0 suppresses scalar writeback but not legal memory reads,
faults or retirement. Load bytes/halfwords sign-extend except LBU/LHU. Stores
take their low 8/16/32 data bits from rs2. PC is an opaque retirement observation.

Ordinary FENCE has opcode 0001111, funct3=000, fm=0; pred/succ use the standard
I/O/R/W bits. This exercise exposes only normal memory R/W: I/O subsets create
no extra device obligations. rd/rs1 are reserved operands ignored as specified
for FENCE; preserve the conservative legal semantics for fm=0. The exact
FENCE.TSO word is legal and is dispatched as a fence, not an ALU no-op or trap.
Other fm values are outside this selected exercise and retire illegal with
cause 2. FENCE.I (funct3=001) is not enabled because Zifencei and an instruction
cache are outside the profile; it must remain distinct and trap with cause 2.
All other unsupported opcode/funct combinations trap with cause 2 and no memory
or scalar write. Illegal words remain illegal even when their operands are zero.

Before issuing a load/store, check natural alignment: halfword address bit 0
and word address bits 1:0 must be zero. Misaligned load/store traps with cause
4/6 and tval equal to effective address, issuing no memory transaction. Response
errors produce cause 5/7 and that same tval. Illegal-instruction tval is the raw
instruction. Successful commands have trap=0, cause=0 and tval=0. Successful
stores and fences never write a scalar destination. No implicit reset or halt
is used to turn a failed instruction into a completed instruction.

## M04. Tagged memory and observable ordering

Memory requests contain unique ID, command tag, original byte address, size
code 0=byte/1=halfword/2=word, write flag and low-byte-aligned store data.
Responses contain the same ID, error, and low-byte-aligned little-endian load
data. The memory BFM applies a successful store and returns a load's memory
value at its response-transfer edge; ready is always high, so a presented
response transfers without a hidden response holding interval. Writes do not
become globally visible merely when a request is queued. Address ranges are
ordinary coherent memory; device/MMIO behavior, caches and speculative external
masters are outside this exercise. Directed tests also use disjoint addresses
to distinguish ordering from same-address forwarding.

For each fence, divide accepted commands into earlier and later instructions.
A selected order edge is satisfied only when every relevant earlier memory
operation has completed its response before a relevant later request is issued
(strictly earlier edge, not the same edge). For fm=0 FENCE, pred R/W crossed
with succ R/W determines the required pairs. Empty predecessor or successor
sets impose no memory-order edge but the fence still retires once.
FENCE.TSO requires earlier loads before later loads and stores (R->R, R->W),
and earlier stores before later stores (W->W). W->R relaxation is permitted,
not required. Implementing TSO as stronger full FENCE RW,RW is correct. Neither
tests nor coverage may require an allowed reordering to occur in a correct
stronger implementation; the relaxation observation is informational only.

Ordinary memory ordering in this reduced exercise preserves overlapping byte
ranges with at least one write in acceptance order: the older access response
is on a strictly earlier clock edge than the younger request, never the same
edge. Byte ranges are compared modulo 2^32, including
address wrap. Different-address reads may issue concurrently
and complete out of order. A conservative implementation may serialize more
operations, subject to the explicit read-concurrency requirement in M06.
Only the oldest unretired command may issue stores; this defines a precise
store side-effect boundary around older exceptions and retirement backpressure.
Loads from younger commands may be outstanding, but their scalar writebacks
remain buffered until their ordered retirement. A trap does not silently retire
or delete younger commands; an explicit flush may cancel them.

## M05. Ordered retirement, flush and reset

Each accepted command produces exactly one retirement in acceptance order,
including fences, rd=x0 instructions, illegal encodings and memory faults.
The retirement packet carries tag, pc, instruction, cancelled, trap, cause,
tval, rd, rd_we and rd_data. Its valid/ready handshake is the sole architectural
scalar-write event. rd_we is false on trap, cancellation, stores, fences or rd=x0.
No younger result can pass a stalled older retirement. Trap/retirement and memory
activity are independently monitored; a completion counter alone is insufficient.

Synchronous flush suppresses command acceptance, new requests and normal
retirement on its edge. Accepted but not retired commands become cancelled
and later retire exactly once in order with no scalar write and no trap.
Cancelled packets have cause=0 and tval=0; unenabled destination fields are ignored.
Already completed stores remain visible; flush does not roll back memory. An
already-accepted store request may still complete and become visible after
flush; no new request is issued for a cancelled command. Outstanding old
responses are drained without scalar writes; do not associate them with reused tags.
Block new command acceptance until cancelled records have retired and old
requests have drained. Repeated flush during drain is idempotent. Reset discards
all records instead, and the BFM discards responses from that reset epoch.
If flush stays low after its last asserted edge and no reset intervenes, the
same ready/response fairness bounds require all cancelled retirements and
draining to complete within 1024 cycles of that edge, with cmd_ready_o restored
by the deadline. A held-valid new command then obeys the four-cycle acceptance
bound. Continually reasserted flush carries no finite recovery claim.

## M06. Capacity, fairness and directed obligations

Outside flush recovery, accept four independent commands into available slots without requiring their
retirement, including while responses or retire_ready are delayed. When a slot
is available and cmd_valid is held high outside flush recovery, accept that command within four cycles.
For the read-concurrency litmus, present two independent aligned loads
back-to-back with no required intervening order edge. Hold mem_req_ready_i=1
and temporarily withhold responses from acceptance of the first load. Within
eight cycles after acceptance of the second command, both read requests must
be accepted. Then release responses, meeting every request's 32-cycle deadline.
Failure to issue the second request within eight cycles fails the litmus;
withholding responses indefinitely is not a valid test. In ordinary tests an
immediate response is legal, without any claim that the second request must
precede it. This finite capacity test forbids using a single blocking
transaction slot as the answer. Do not require multiple
outstanding stores or force the optional TSO W->R relaxation.

For liveness tests the environment supplies ready at least once per eight
cycles and a response within 32 cycles for every issued request. Every accepted
non-flushed command then retires within 1024 cycles. No bounded-liveness claim
is made without those assumptions. Directed obligations include TSO legality,
all three required order pairs, ordinary fence masks including empty masks,
back-to-back fences, older delayed stores plus younger loads, out-of-order load
responses, rd=x0, all access sizes/sign modes, misalignment, bus error, illegal
nearby encodings, tag reuse, retire stalls and flush/reset races. Resetting the
DUT to escape a fence wait fails the progress obligation.

## M07. Cadence implementation and acceptance

Deliver synthesizable standard SV, explicit package/file ordering and a pure-SV
UVM environment. Required roles are command sequencer/driver, memory responder,
passive request/response/retirement monitors, a byte-memory and instruction
scoreboard, an order-edge scoreboard, SVA and TP-linked covergroups. The expected
model is independently derived from M03-M06 and the applicable ISA clauses;
do not read the candidate RTL to define expected behavior. Check behavior-changing
mutations for illegal TSO decode, fence treated as a no-op, violation of an R->W
edge (bypassing other serialization when needed), swapped response
ID, duplicate retirement, wrong sign extension and dropped flush cancellation.
Each mutation must create an observable contract violation; document
semantically equivalent/redundant edits as inapplicable negative controls.
Legal stronger ordering must not be labelled a surviving bug mutation.

Freeze applicable functional bins before the first run: decoded instruction
class, fence pred/succ masks, all mandatory order pairs, load/store size and
alignment, error class, rd=x0, tag reuse, queue occupancy, response permutation,
ready-pressure phase, reset/flush phase. Mandatory crosses include fence class
x required pair x delayed predecessor, fence x retirement stall, and flush x
pending response. An optional W->R-reordering bin cannot be placed in the
mandatory denominator. Require >90% applicable functional bins, all directed
obligations, all declared mutation detections and no unexpected UVM/SVA errors.
Report RTL code/toggle and assertion coverage separately.

Xcelium compiles and runs the direct SV/UVM closure; IMC consumes its native
coverage database. Use Jasper Superlint/CDC/FPV with explicit clock/reset and
fairness assumptions, and Genus for RTL elaboration/synthesizability. This is a
single-clock interface; CDC evidence must say so rather than fabricate a
crossing. None of these stages requires proprietary VIP or upstream build tools.
The exported kit contains `eda/cadence_runner.py` inspect/plan/run and
`eda/verification_profile.json`; supply that file to `dv_generate_uvm`.
Put the actual candidate and TB inventory in `eda/project.json`, with fixed
seeds, constraints, raw tool outputs, coverage model and input hashes. The EDA
host supplies Cadence binaries/licenses. This package has not been compiled,
simulated or formally proven on that host; source closure checks are not signoff.

## Exact interface assets

These definitions are the complete authored ABI; they are included in source contexts.

### contracts/coral_memory_order_contract_pkg.sv

```systemverilog
// SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
// Authored interface contract only; no implementation or verification oracle.
package coral_memory_order_contract_pkg;
  localparam int XLEN = 32;
  localparam int COMMAND_SLOTS = 4;
  localparam int READ_SLOTS = 4;
  localparam logic [31:0] FENCE_TSO = 32'h8330000f;
  typedef struct packed {
    logic [7:0] tag;
    logic [31:0] pc;
    logic [31:0] instruction;
    logic [31:0] rs1;
    logic [31:0] rs2;
  } memory_command_t;
  typedef struct packed {
    logic [7:0] id;
    logic [7:0] tag;
    logic write;
    logic [31:0] address;
    logic [1:0] size;
    logic [31:0] data;
  } memory_request_t;
  typedef struct packed {
    logic [7:0] id;
    logic error;
    logic [31:0] data;
  } memory_response_t;
  typedef struct packed {
    logic [7:0] tag;
    logic [31:0] pc;
    logic [31:0] instruction;
    logic cancelled;
    logic trap;
    logic [4:0] cause;
    logic [31:0] tval;
    logic [4:0] rd;
    logic rd_we;
    logic [31:0] rd_data;
  } memory_retirement_t;
endpackage
```

### contracts/coral_memory_order_ports.svh

```systemverilog
// SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
// Include inside module coral_memory_order_subsystem(...).
input  logic clk_i,
input  logic rst_ni,
input  logic flush_i,
input  logic cmd_valid_i,
output logic cmd_ready_o,
input  coral_memory_order_contract_pkg::memory_command_t cmd_i,
output logic mem_req_valid_o,
input  logic mem_req_ready_i,
output coral_memory_order_contract_pkg::memory_request_t mem_req_o,
input  logic mem_rsp_valid_i,
output logic mem_rsp_ready_o,
input  coral_memory_order_contract_pkg::memory_response_t mem_rsp_i,
output logic retire_valid_o,
input  logic retire_ready_i,
output coral_memory_order_contract_pkg::memory_retirement_t retire_o
```
